interest: This file offers a remarkable window into the early Allied Occupation of Japan, showing how mundane questions of housing and rent intersected with high-level international economic policy, military logistics, and post-war legal dilemmas. It provides poignant micro-historical evidence of the plight of elderly pre-war foreign residents—most notably Annie Harloe/Harllee, widow of Robert Young, founder and editor of the influential Japan Chronicle—who was left impoverished in San Francisco at age 74 while American occupation personnel occupied her Shioya villa, completely barred from receiving rental payments due to strict Treasury controls under the Trading with the Enemy Act. Additionally, the file captures the bureaucratic turf boundaries between the State Department and the War Department over military dependent housing, as well as SCAP's intricate logistical planning (culminating in SCAPIN 1839) to billet foreign commercial buyers in designated control points (Tokyo-Yokohama, Kyoto, Osaka, Nagoya) without straining the war-ravaged Japanese economy or violating strict currency exchange regulations.
overview: Decimal file 894.502 covers housing, dwellings, rents, and living conditions in occupied Japan from October 1946 through August 1948. The file contains four main groups of material: personal petitions from American citizens regarding pre-war property in Japan, prominently Mrs. Annie Harloe (Harllee), widow of Robert Young (former editor and publisher of the Japan Chronicle), who sought rental income from her requisitioned estate in Shioya, Kobe, but was repeatedly rebuffed due to War Department jurisdiction and foreign exchange prohibitions under the Trading with the Enemy Act; congressional correspondence from Representative Lindley Beckworth regarding dependent housing shortages for U.S. Air Corps personnel at Fuchu; detailed State Department and SCAP planning documents concerning logistical support, billeting, hotel accommodations, transportation, and currency arrangements for the reopening of Japan to private international trade representatives (including SCAPIN 1839); and diplomatic despatches from the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo transmitting an Economic and Scientific Section (ESS) survey on post-war Japanese housing requirements.

subfiles.about: Mrs. Annie Harloe writes to the Secretary of State requesting permission to rent her home in Shioya, Kobe, which is currently occupied by American citizens, in order to pay for living expenses.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Annie Harloe writes from San Francisco to inquire whether it is possible to rent out her home located in Shioya, a suburb of Kobe, Japan, which she understands is currently occupied by U.S. citizens. She explains that all her assets remain tied up in Japan and that an earlier claim submitted through the State Department has yielded no compensation. Experiencing financial hardship, she urgently requests assistance in obtaining monthly rental payments to cover her current living expenses.
subfiles.title: Letter from Annie Harloe to the Secretary of State regarding rental of home in Shioya, Kobe

subfiles.about: The State Department outlines the citizenship documentation needed to investigate Mrs. Harloe's property and explains that Treasury and occupation regulations strictly prohibit the transfer of rental funds from Japan.
subfiles.from: James W. Gantenbein, Assistant Chief, Division of Foreign Service Administration, For the Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: The Department of State acknowledges Mrs. Harloe's letter of October 5, 1946, advising her to submit a sworn statement in quadruplicate and proof of American citizenship so that the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo can be asked to investigate the property. However, the letter explains that under Treasury Department regulations pursuant to the Trading with the Enemy Act and Theater foreign exchange controls, rental funds cannot be transferred from Japan to the United States. It notes that due to severe foreign exchange shortages required for essential imports, dollar balances will not be available for capital transfers in the foreseeable future.
subfiles.title: Letter from State Department (Foreign Service Administration) to Annie Harloe regarding property status and currency transfer prohibitions

subfiles.about: An internal handwritten note cautions that another State Department office had previously responded to an inquiry on the Harloe property and advises locating previous correspondence.
subfiles.summary: An informal handwritten memorandum advises colleagues to retrieve earlier case records concerning Mrs. Harloe before dispatching further communications. The writer warns that another departmental office had answered an earlier letter with differing information. It emphasizes the necessity of reviewing previous files to avoid issuing contradictory responses.
subfiles.title: State Department handwritten internal routing note on Harloe correspondence

subfiles.about: The Office of the Legal Adviser requests the Division of Foreign Service Administration to check for and forward previous correspondence charged out in the Harloe case.
subfiles.from: A.O.F., Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.summary: The Office of the Legal Adviser writes to the Division of Foreign Service Administration (FA) concerning a previous communication dated July 10, 1946 charged out to FA on November 1. FA is asked to locate the document and send both it and the attached papers to Benedict M. English in Room 314-W. This reflects internal administrative efforts to consolidate the file on Mrs. Harloe's inquiries.
subfiles.title: Office of the Legal Adviser routing slip regarding previous Harloe correspondence

subfiles.about: Benedict M. English indicates that the Harloe file is temporarily missing and advises forwarding the current papers.
subfiles.from: Benedict M. English (M B Engles), Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.summary: Benedict M. English of the Legal Adviser's office returns a routing slip stating that the case file is not currently in his possession. He directs the staff to send the incoming correspondence onward rather than delay it. He notes that he will be glad to conduct another search for the missing file at a later time.
subfiles.title: Office of the Legal Adviser routing slip from Benedict M. English regarding missing case file

subfiles.about: Mrs. Annie Harllee sends a follow-up inquiry regarding rental income from her home in Shioya, identifying it as the property of her late husband Robert Young of the Japan Chronicle.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Annie Harllee writes to the Facilities Branch of the State Department stating that she has received no reply to her letter sent a month earlier regarding her home in Shioya near Kobe. She reveals that the property is registered in the name of her late husband, Mr. Robert Young, former owner and editor of the Japan Chronicle, and is currently requisitioned and occupied by American occupation forces. Explaining that she is 74 years old and running out of money while all her assets remain tied up in Japan, she pleads for permission to obtain monthly rental income to meet current living expenses.
subfiles.title: Letter from Annie Harllee to Facilities Branch regarding property of late husband Robert Young in Shioya
subfiles.to: Facilities Branch, State Department, Washington, D.C.

subfiles.about: The Office of the Legal Adviser informs Mrs. Harloe that requisitioned properties fall under War Department jurisdiction and that existing regulations prohibit transferring rental payments from Japan.
subfiles.from: Benedict M. English, Assistant to the Legal Adviser, For the Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Benedict M. English replies to Mrs. Harloe's letter of November 6, 1946 regarding her home near Kobe occupied by American forces. He explains that rental compensation for property requisitioned for the use of U.S. forces is primarily the responsibility of the War Department. Furthermore, he emphasizes that even if the property is requisitioned and funds are appropriated, existing occupation regulations provide no mechanism for transferring funds out of Japan, making it impossible to remit any rental payments to her in the United States.
subfiles.title: Letter from Benedict M. English to Annie Harloe regarding War Department jurisdiction and fund transfers

subfiles.about: Representative Lindley Beckworth transmits a constituent letter from Mrs. Nolan E. Herrington requesting assistance in obtaining dependent housing at Fuchu, Japan.
subfiles.summary: Congressman Lindley Beckworth forwards an excerpt from a letter by Mrs. Nolan E. Herrington of New London, Texas, whose husband, 1st Lt. Nolan E. Herrington (Air Corps), was recently transferred from Manila to Fuchu, Japan. Mrs. Herrington complains that despite waiting ten months to join him, Fuchu lacks dependent housing facilities even though convertible buildings exist on the base. Beckworth strongly endorses the Herringtons and requests that the State Department look into possibilities for facilitating her travel to Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from Representative Lindley Beckworth regarding dependent housing for Lt. Nolan E. Herrington at Fuchu

subfiles.about: The State Department informs Representative Beckworth that housing and travel for military dependents are outside its jurisdiction and have been referred to the War Department.
subfiles.from: John M. Allison, Acting Chief, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs, For the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: John M. Allison responds to Representative Beckworth's letter of March 1, 1947 regarding Mrs. N. E. Herrington's request to join her husband at Fuchu, Japan. Allison clarifies that matters involving Army officers and their dependents fall outside the jurisdiction of the Department of State. He informs Beckworth that the inquiry has been forwarded to the War Department, which holds primary responsibility, and notes that a direct response will be forthcoming from that agency.
subfiles.title: Letter from John M. Allison to Representative Lindley Beckworth regarding War Department jurisdiction over military housing
subfiles.to: The Honorable Lindley Beckworth, House of Representatives

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum and draft cable to SCAP analyze logistical arrangements and formulate policy questions concerning housing, transportation, and currency for visiting private trade representatives.
subfiles.from: Mr. Whitman (JK - Division of Japanese-Korean Economic Affairs)
subfiles.summary: This five-page memorandum and draft outgoing cable analyze SCAP's May 10, 1947 plan for reopening Japan to limited private trade, focusing on Part III concerning logistical support. It details SCAP plans to provide hotel quarters and meals in Tokyo-Yokohama, Kyoto, Osaka, and Nagoya, along with rail and taxi transport, recreation at the American Club of Tokyo, and medical facilities on a revenue basis. The attached draft cable asks SCAP Headquarters five critical policy questions concerning daily lodging rates, acceptable currencies, exchange rates, SCAP trade account revenues, office rental under the 50:1 conversion rate, property restitution for commercial representatives, and proposed simultaneous press releases in Washington and Tokyo.
subfiles.title: State Department Office Memorandum and draft telegram to SCAP regarding accommodations and logistical arrangements for private trade representatives in Japan

subfiles.about: The U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo transmits SCAPIN 1839 directing the Japanese Government to provide office space and housing for commercial representatives and licensees.
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo (drafted by R. H. Bushner)
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 36 from the Office of the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo forwards five copies of SCAPIN 1839, dated December 31, 1947, entitled 'Accommodations for Semi-Permanent Commercial Representatives and Licensees.' The directive instructs the Japanese Government to arrange offices and housing for commercial representatives permitted to remain in Japan on a semi-permanent basis. Payment for these accommodations is to be made in acceptable foreign exchange subject to the approval of the ESS Foreign Trade Division, and facilities released by Occupation Forces may be repurposed for commercial rental.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 36 from Political Adviser (Tokyo) transmitting SCAPIN 1839 on housing and offices for commercial representatives
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.

subfiles.about: The U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo transmits a comprehensive research report prepared by SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section on post-war Japanese housing requirements.
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo (drafted by J. D. Edwards)
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 513 from the Office of the U.S. Political Adviser for Japan transmits two copies of a research report entitled 'Japanese Housing Requirements, June 1948,' prepared by the Research and Programs Division of SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section (ESS). The report provides a systematic analysis of Japan's post-war housing deficit caused by wartime bombing, repatriation, and population growth. The despatch officially places the research findings into State Department economic records.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 513 from Political Adviser (Tokyo) transmitting ESS report on Japanese Housing Requirements
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.
